challenges.name: graceful-shutdown-quiz
challenges.title: Read the 502s of every rollout
challenges.description: Three statements about the burst of 502s the ingress logged each time the gateway was rolled out. Decide whether each one is true.
hints: Read the documentation of `http.Server.Shutdown` and `http.Server.Close` side by side: what happens to a request that is half-way through its handler in each case?
SIGTERM and the removal from the Service's endpoints are both triggered by the pod being deleted. Is one of them guaranteed to happen before the other, everywhere in the cluster?
Look up what the kubelet does when `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` runs out and the process is still alive.

questions.question:
The gateway's first shutdown handler:

```go
sig := make(chan os.Signal, 1)
signal.Notify(sig, syscall.SIGTERM)
<-sig
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Second)
defer cancel()
srv.Shutdown(ctx)
```

Statement: "`srv.Shutdown` closes every open connection at once, like `srv.Close`, so requests in flight at that moment fail; the 20-second context only limits how long closing takes."
questions.explanation: False. `Shutdown` first closes the listeners (no new connections), then closes idle connections and waits for active ones to become idle, that is, for the requests in flight to finish; the context bounds that wait, and when it expires `Shutdown` returns its error so you can decide what to do next. `Close` is the one that cuts active connections at once. (Hijacked connections such as WebSockets are not tracked; `RegisterOnShutdown` is how you tell them to finish.) The misconception is that a graceful shutdown means closing faster.

questions.question:
Ingress logs during a rollout, with the old gateway pod `gateway-7c9f` receiving SIGTERM at 10:04:00.000:

```text
10:04:00.412 upstream=10.8.1.14:8080 (gateway-7c9f) status=502 connect() failed (111: Connection refused)
10:04:01.207 upstream=10.8.1.14:8080 (gateway-7c9f) status=502 connect() failed (111: Connection refused)
10:04:02.950 upstream=10.8.1.14:8080 (gateway-7c9f) status=502 connect() failed (111: Connection refused)
10:04:03.300 (no more requests routed to 10.8.1.14)
```

Statement: "Removing the pod from the endpoints and sending SIGTERM happen in parallel, so for a few seconds after SIGTERM the load balancers still send new connections; the gateway should keep serving for a short delay (or use a preStop sleep) before it closes its listener."
questions.explanation: True. Deleting a pod starts both the SIGTERM to its containers and its removal from EndpointSlices; kube-proxy, the ingress controller and cloud load balancers learn about the removal at their own pace. A process that closes its listener immediately refuses the connections that still arrive, and the ingress turns them into 502s. A delay before `Shutdown` (in the app or as a `preStop` hook) bridges that window. The misconception is that Kubernetes stops traffic before it sends SIGTERM.

questions.question:
The deployment sets `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30`. A stuck report export kept the gateway's `Shutdown` waiting:

```text
10:04:00  SIGTERM received, draining
10:04:05  listener closed, waiting for 1 request
10:04:30  (pod gone)
$ kubectl -n rice-rocket get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=gateway-7c9f
Normal  Killing  pod/gateway-7c9f  Stopping container gateway
```

Statement: "When the 30 seconds run out, the kubelet sends SIGTERM a second time and waits another grace period, so a shutdown that takes 45 seconds still finishes cleanly."
questions.explanation: False. When the grace period ends and the container is still running, the kubelet sends SIGKILL: no handler runs, buffered logs are lost and the workers stop mid-job. The shutdown must fit inside the grace period with a margin, which is why the `Shutdown` context gets a budget (grace period minus the drain delay, the time to stop the workers and a margin), and a request that would overrun it is cut on purpose. The misconception is that the grace period is a polite reminder.

challenges.name: gateway-graceful-shutdown
challenges.title: Shut the gateway down without dropping requests
challenges.description: Every rollout of the gateway produced a burst of 502s, and once a stuck request kept a pod alive until SIGKILL, losing the last logs and a half-processed job. The editor holds `shutdown.go`, the SIGTERM handler, with its key blocks missing, each marked by a `// [ ]` line; some pieces are wrong on purpose. Fill every line so that the gateway: keeps serving for `DrainDelayMs` while the load balancers stop sending traffic; then stops accepting and waits for the requests in flight, but only for the time left in the grace period after the drain delay, the worker stop and a safety margin; stops the background workers and flushes the logs; and exits 0 when every request finished or 1 when one had to be cut. Run replays rollouts against a simulated pod with a virtual clock.
hints: Draw the 30 seconds after SIGTERM on a line: when do new requests stop arriving, when may the listener close, and what must still fit after the last request before SIGKILL?
Look at the order of the calls on `g`, at the timeout passed to `Shutdown` (what is left of `GracePeriodMs`), and at what decides the exit code.

A queue consumer with the same shape: `g.Sleep(cfg.PauseMs)` to let the broker reassign partitions, `err := g.Drain(cfg.GraceMs - cfg.PauseMs - cfg.CommitMs - cfg.MarginMs)`, `g.CommitOffsets(); g.CloseProducer()`, then `if err != nil { g.Exit(1); return }; g.Exit(0)`.

tests.name: A rollout: every request in flight or still routed to the pod is served
A slow 8-second report export finishes before the pod exits
A stuck request is cut at the deadline; the pod still exits 1 before SIGKILL
Requests routed in the first 3 seconds after SIGTERM are not refused
